title: Deques
content:
# Deques A queue allows removal only at the front and insertion only at the rear. As shown below, a double-ended queue, or deque, is more flexible: elements can be added or removed at either end. ![Deque operations](deque.assets/deque_operations.svg) ## Common deque operations The table below lists common operations. Actual method names depend on the programming language.

Table   Efficiency of deque operations

| Method | Description | Time complexity | | -------------- | ---------------- | ---------- | | `push_first()` | Add an element at the front | $O(1)$ | | `push_last()` | Add an element at the rear | $O(1)$ | | `pop_first()` | Remove the front element | $O(1)$ | | `pop_last()` | Remove the rear element | $O(1)$ | | `peek_first()` | Access the front element | $O(1)$ | | `peek_last()` | Access the rear element | $O(1)$ | Again, we can use a deque class already provided by the programming language: ```snippet deque_operations ``` ??? pythontutor "Visualize execution" @tutor deque_operations_tutor ## Implementing a deque * A deque is implemented much like a queue, using either a linked list or an array as the underlying structure. ### Implementation with a doubly linked list In the previous section, we used a singly linked list for a queue because it easily supports removing the head for dequeueing and adding after the tail for enqueueing. A deque supports both insertion and removal at both ends. It therefore needs the symmetric operations in the other direction as well. For this reason, we use a doubly linked list. As shown below, treat the list's head and tail as the deque's front and rear, and support adding and removing nodes at both ends. === "<1>" ![Insertion and removal in a linked-list deque](deque.assets/linkedlist_deque_step1.svg) === "<2>" ![linkedlist_deque_push_last](deque.assets/linkedlist_deque_step2_push_last.svg) === "<3>" ![linkedlist_deque_push_first](deque.assets/linkedlist_deque_step3_push_first.svg) === "<4>" ![linkedlist_deque_pop_last](deque.assets/linkedlist_deque_step4_pop_last.svg) === "<5>" ![linkedlist_deque_pop_first](deque.assets/linkedlist_deque_step5_pop_first.svg) The implementation is as follows: ```src [file]{linkedlist_deque}-[class]{linked_list_deque}-[func]{} ``` ### Implementation with an array As with an array-based queue, we can use a circular array to implement a deque, as shown below. === "<1>" ![Insertion and removal in an array-based deque](deque.assets/array_deque_step1.svg) === "<2>" ![array_deque_push_last](deque.assets/array_deque_step2_push_last.svg) === "<3>" ![array_deque_push_first](deque.assets/array_deque_step3_push_first.svg) === "<4>" ![array_deque_pop_last](deque.assets/array_deque_step4_pop_last.svg) === "<5>" ![array_deque_pop_first](deque.assets/array_deque_step5_pop_first.svg) Starting with the queue implementation, we need only add methods for insertion at the front and removal at the rear: ```src [file]{array_deque}-[class]{array_deque}-[func]{} ``` ## Applications A deque combines stack and queue behavior, **so it supports all their applications while offering greater flexibility**. Software undo is usually implemented with a stack: the system uses `push` to record each change and `pop` to undo it. Because resources are limited, software often restricts the history to a fixed number of steps, such as $50$. When the stack grows beyond $50$, the oldest entry must be removed from the bottom, the front of the deque. **A stack cannot provide this operation, so a deque is needed instead**. The core undo behavior still follows last-in, first-out order; the deque simply provides flexibility for the additional logic.
